Your front end on http://localhost:5173 calls your API on http://localhost:8080, and the console says:

Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' from origin 'http://localhost:5173'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present
on the requested resource.

The request often reached the server and got an answer. The browser refused to hand the answer to your code. Here's why, and what to change.

Origins and the Same-Origin Policy

An origin is the scheme, host and port of a URL together:

URL A URL B Same origin? Why
https://app.example.com https://app.example.com/x Yes Only the path differs
https://example.com http://example.com No Scheme
https://example.com https://api.example.com No Host
http://localhost:5173 http://localhost:8080 No Port

By default, a page's JavaScript can only read responses from its own origin. That's the same-origin policy. Without it, any site you visit could call fetch("https://yourbank.com/account"): your browser would attach your bank cookies, and the page would read your balance.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server opts out, for the origins it trusts.

The Header That Fixes Most Cases

For a simple GET, the browser sends the request with an Origin header, and checks the response:

GET /api/users HTTP/1.1
Origin: http://localhost:5173
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Content-Type: application/json

If Access-Control-Allow-Origin matches the page's origin, or is *, your code gets the response. Otherwise it gets a network error, and the details are only in the console.

Preflight Requests

Some requests could change data on servers that never expected cross-origin calls. For those, the browser first asks permission with an OPTIONS request, the preflight:

OPTIONS /api/users/42 HTTP/1.1
Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization

The server must answer with what it allows:

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, authorization
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600

Only then does the browser send the real PUT. Access-Control-Max-Age lets it cache the answer, here for 10 minutes, so it doesn't preflight every call.

A request skips the preflight only when it's "simple": method GET, HEAD or POST, no custom headers, and a Content-Type of text/plain, multipart/form-data or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. So sending JSON with Content-Type: application/json, or an Authorization header, always triggers a preflight.

Cookies and Credentials

By default, cross-origin fetch sends no cookies. To send them:

fetch("https://api.example.com/me", { credentials: "include" });

The server must then answer with both:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

With credentials, * is not allowed: the origin must be named exactly. Cookies also need SameSite=None; Secure to be sent cross-site at all.

Setting It Up on the Server

In Express, with the cors package:

import cors from "cors";

app.use(
  cors({
    origin: ["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:5173"],
    credentials: true,
  }),
);

In Spring Boot:

@Configuration
public class CorsConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
            .allowedOrigins("https://app.example.com")
            .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE")
            .allowCredentials(true);
    }
}

If you list several origins by hand, send back only the one that matches the request's Origin, and add Vary: Origin so caches don't serve one origin's answer to another. The libraries above do both.

In Development: Use a Proxy

Often the simplest fix is to make the calls same-origin. Vite can forward /api to your back end:

// vite.config.js
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: { "/api": "http://localhost:8080" },
  },
};

Your code calls fetch("/api/users"), the browser sees one origin, and CORS never comes up. In production, a reverse proxy like nginx serving the app and the API on the same domain does the same.

Common Errors and Their Fix

Console message says Fix
No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header Send it from the server, on errors too (a 500 often lacks it)
Response to preflight doesn't pass access control Answer OPTIONS with 2xx and the allow headers; check auth isn't blocking it
Header authorization not allowed Add it to Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Wildcard * with credentials mode include Name the exact origin and send Allow-Credentials: true
Value doesn't equal the supplied origin Check scheme, port and trailing slash: https://a.com/ is wrong

What CORS Does Not Do

  • It doesn't protect your API. curl, Postman and other servers ignore CORS completely. Authentication and authorization still do the protecting.
  • It doesn't stop the request. For simple requests, the server runs the code; the browser only hides the answer. That's why state-changing endpoints also need CSRF protection when they use cookies.
  • "Disable CORS" browser extensions only hide the problem on your machine. Your users won't have them.

The Answer in Short

  1. An origin is scheme + host + port; pages can read only their own origin's responses by default.
  2. The server allows others with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  3. JSON bodies and custom headers trigger a preflight OPTIONS the server must answer.
  4. With cookies, name the exact origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
  5. In development, a dev-server proxy avoids CORS entirely.
